utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First, I want to say good afternoon to the interpreters and ask me whether they hear me? They do. We can continue. Mr Harmon, the floor is yours. This is going to be a busy week. We will try to organise a status conference. You had some scheduling concerns. We will try to do everything we can. The Trial Chamber has other cases that it is hearing as well. I have a status conference tomorrow in the Kordic case. There are motions that were filed by the Defence, which should not be discussed here. We have to review them. All of this means that we have to try to keep speeding up, as much as possible, the witnesses, but without prejudice to the rights of the Defence or to the Prosecution. Mr Harmon, I now give you the floor to continue the testimony of Mr Mesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, if Mr Mesic could be brought in, Mr President, I will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can I have the witness brought in, please? (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Mesic, good afternoon. Are you rested, are you feeling well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr Harmon. STJEPAN MESIC (continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr Mesic. Let me first of all ask you, could you describe to the judges when you met Franjo Tudjman and could you describe your social and professional relationship with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had the honour to meet Franjo Tudjman earlier -- that was in 1970 or before 1970, but this was at Matica Hrvatska and we did not really associate specifically at that time. I came to know him better during the Croatian Spring, and even better subsequently, after we returned from the prison -- we would find ourselves in social circles which were -- which happened because of certain birthdays or some other social occasions, because we could not call these meetings political meetings, but we found ways to meet. We were all leaders of the Croatian Spring, then the generals who retired from the service in the former JNA due to Croatian nationalism and in such circles Franjo Tudjman would also be there very frequently. I do not know what else you may be interested, in that regard, in regard of our association.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr Mesic, as part of the Government both of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and in Government in the Republic of Yugoslavia, did you have contacts with Franjo Tudjman, and can you describe those contacts, the frequency of contacts, the type, the nature of those contacts, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During these occasions when we met, we would discuss the topical events of that particular point in time. We analysed the situation in the former Yugoslavia, in Croatia, we analysed what was going on in the world, and we would try to forecast what the situation was going to look like, where it was going to go and what we could do in that regard, and I need to say, with respect to Franjo Tudjman, he always took part in such discussions, but he was not easy to talk with, because he did not very well tolerant the differences in views. He was not a pleasant collocateur -- he was very hard in his positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr Mesic, during your contacts with President Tudjman, did he ever express his views in respect of Bosnia, and, if he did, could you tell the judges what his views were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that one can read on that in his books, but, to put it succinctly, in these discussions and elsewhere, and when speaking in public, his position was that, after World War II, it was a big mistake to have created Bosnia as a republic. He believed that Bosnia should not have been structured in such a way as a separate republic, but that, instead, it should have been dealt with like Kosovo and Vojvodina, which were annexed to Serbia. He thought that the best course of action would have been for the Bosniaks, given their origin, because it is believed that they are for the most part Croats, so it would have been best that Bosnia should have been annexed to Croatia, but that some modality should have been found in that respect, so Bosnia should have been associated with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were the views that he expressed to you about the annexing of Bosnia to Croatia, were those long held views, firmly held views?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that his initial positions were really a critique of the Communist leadership, which had allowed that Bosnia be created as a separate entity, that is, a constituent part of Yugoslavia, so at first, during our conversation, it did not come out that this position should have been changed. Even after Croatia became independent, this idea was not really tabled about the restructuring of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You could only glean that from certain statements regarding the very strange shape of Croatia. It was considered that this shape of Croatia, which looks like a crescent -- it was considered that certain parts are missing, but there were no serious discussions in which way the position of Bosnia should be changed. But, as time went by, and if Yugoslavia was going to disappear and it was a multi-national State, how Bosnia was going to survive as a multi-national State. It was believed that it would be very difficult to keep it alive and these were positions that were then expressed publicly, but also it was something that was discussed in inner circles as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In those discussions, both publicly and in inner circles, did he express a view that parts of Bosnia, historically, belonged to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believed that Tudjman's position was that the best position for Croatia and for the entire area was the solution from 1938, which was Banovina Croatia and the borders of the Banovina were defined then. However, this Banovina never really fully came alive, because of the World War II -- the process was interrupted and now, obviously, part of this Banovina was now within the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. This was 1938 -- you mean 1938, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was at that time that the Banovina was created in 1938, but then World War II came and Banovina never fully came alive. Then, after World War II, Yugoslavia was recreated, but now not as a unitary State but as a Federal State, which comprised Serbia, Croatia and then Macedonia, Slovenia and Montenegro as well and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: His views were the territory that was comprised in the Banovina should be annexed to or absorbed into Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, his position was that this would have been logical, because there would have been fewer conflicts this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did he ever express to you, either in your discourse socially or in your business communications, his views about Muslims in Bosnia, and could you explain what those views were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that his positions are fairly well known, that is, with respect to the Bosniak Muslims. He thought that they were Croats by origin, that they converted to Islam during the Turkish occupation. However, as the situation developed, after the independence of Croatia, I believe that there were some unclear points. If they were Croats by origin, I think that we should have cooperated more closely with them, because we were both the victims of the same aggression. However, later, the conflict broke out between the Croats and Muslims, which was damaging to these victims of the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he ever express his views about Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am personally familiar with Alija Izetbegovic because we both formed the Defence counsel in the former system. I must say Alija Izetbegovic is a wise man, but he is not a person who is skilled in politics -- he is not a dominating person. He entered politics -- he was catapulted into the politics. I think that he did not have such clear ideas at first and I think Franjo Tudjman was aware of this, so that he could approach Alija Izetbegovic with more, how shall I put it -- you know, he is a general, after all, but he treated him in a way that is not really appropriate -- he treated him as if he did not know enough about politics, so he was a bit condescending to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And so General Tudjman essentially was -- let me ask you a different question. Mr Mesic, President Tudjman was in fact a former general in the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what you are saying is that that tempered his views towards Mr Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think that he had kind of moderate views to Izetbegovic. I think that he may have underestimated Alija Izetbegovic, because he did not really appear to him as a politician. At first, maybe he did not, but he was a smart man. He found himself in this situation. He was elected to President of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina at a time when -- at the height of the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina. He had no defence mechanisms at his disposal, so that he may have made moves that were incomprehensible to Tudjman, but on the other hand the situation of Alija Izetbegovic was very difficult. To me, it was really a situation that offered no good solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr Mesic, can you describe a meeting that took place between President Tudjman and President Milosevic -- that took place in 1991 at Karadordevo . Can you tell the judges what you know about that meeting and what the ramifications of that meeting were in respect of Croatian policy toward Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that this meeting at Karadordevo was sort of a turning point -- when the policy was changed -- the policy, when it was first believed that there was no Bosnia without Croatia and vice versa, and after this meeting, what was taken into account was the initial successes of Serbia. I must say that this was at first tolerated by the European entities and I think that the observers may have perceived that Bosnia was finished and that it was doomed and I think that it was from this situation that Tudjman was drawing his conclusions. As far as the meeting at Karadordevo itself is concerned, at that time I was a member of the Presidency of Yugoslavia and, in discussions with Bora Jovic, who was the Serb representative in the Presidency in Yugoslavia, I said, "We in Croatia have information that the Serb villages," that is, the villages mostly populated by the Serbs "are being armed; that they are being armed by the JNA" -- which was becoming more and more Serb, because we must bear in mind that Yugoslavia functioned and it had three integrating factors. One was Tito and his charisma; one was JNA; and one was the Communist League -- the Communist Party that is. While these three elements were around, Yugoslavia could functions fairly successfully. Once Tito disappeared from the scene, and after Milosevic destroyed the Communist Party, which was Yugoslav but mostly dominated by the Serbs, he then took control of the JNA so that the JNA became dominated by Milosevic and put itself in his service. This is why out of their depots the Serb population was being armed. I told Bora Jovic, the Serb President in the Presidency, that we have this information, that it was a suicidal policy on the part of Serbs in Croatia as well as the Serbs overall and that, in any ensuing conflict, they will lose the most, because 10 per cent of the Serb population cannot resist the 90 per cent, because then the Croats would arm themselves and a catastrophe would ensue and the most damage will befall the Serbs. I asked them what did they want. He said that they were not interested in the Serbs in Croatia, that they were our citizens, that we could do whatever we wanted with them and that they were also not interested in the Croatian territories, that is the territories of the Croatian State. I said, "Well, what are you interested in?" He said then that they were interested in Serbia in 66 per cent of Bosnia. He said this used to be Serbia and this will remain Serb. Since they were not interested in Croatia, that is the Croatian territory, or the Serbs in Croatia, then I said, "Why do we not sit down? Why do we not try to avoid a war? People are being armed and everything and everything could blow up. There is no need to shed blood if we can sit down and resolve things at the table." He said that he agreed, but he needed to talk to Slobodan Milosevic. I said that I would talk to Tudjman and I said, "Why do not the four of us sit down at the table and see what the problems of the Serbs in Croatia were so that we could resolve things without any armed conflict, because we have an opportunity to do so". I knew that there was such an opportunity, because, as a Prime Minister in 1990, I attempted to establish contacts with the representatives of the municipalities where the population was Serb -- the majority of the population was Serb, and at that time all these representatives wanted to discuss, with the exception of Milan Babic, who was the president of the municipality in Knin. He was directly in contact with Belgrade and he personally forbid this contact. But I could see that people did want peaceful resolution of the problem, and I also said that the Bosnian problem should be resolved on an international level, that it should be internationalised, that it should be resolved through the UN, but that we should do everything to avoid a war. Since Slobodan Milosevic agreed to the meeting and he said that we could meet anywhere, State-side or abroad, then I went to Zagreb and I talked to Franjo Tudjman and told him that these two men were agreeable and was he agreeable that we should all sit down and he said that he was. Then I expected this call to see when we could organise this meeting. However, Tudjman, at one point, told us that he was going to go to Karadordevo alone -- this was on 30 March of 1991 -- that he wanted to see what they wanted. I objected to Karadordevo, because Tito held the 21st session there of the Communist Party and this is when the Croatian Spring was broken, so I said, "We should not go to this place because we have bad memories relating to it". He said it did not matter where we meet; it is more important to find out what they wanted. Tudjman came back from Karadordevo that same day and he told us that the army was not going to attack us, that he had guarantees of Veljoko Kadijevic, who was the Chief-of-Staff, and of Milosevic, and that it would be difficult for Bosnia to survive, that we could get borders of the Banovina. Tudjman also said that Milosevic, sort of in a gesture of largesse -- that Croatia could take Cazin, Kladusa and Bihac, because this was the so-called Turkish Croatia and the Serbs did not need it. I thought Milosevic was really dolling out foreign territories and I said this would end up in catastrophe. I objected and this is why I was later given a lot of grief for that, but then I also said that there would be a short war in Slovenia, a longer one in Croatia and that Bosnia would be awash in blood and, unfortunately, I seem to have been right on all these counts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr Mesic, from that day forward, did Croatian policy vis-à-vis Bosnia change? Was there in fact a dual policy then from Croatia towards Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Croatian public policy always proceeded from the position that Bosnia was a State, that it was unified, and that Croatia was the first to have recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, in objective terms, taking into account everything that happened subsequently, when Milosevic created a Serb republic within the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croats formed the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which later became the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, it became clear that this did not consolidate Bosnia-Herzegovina, but, on the contrary, it undermined it, especially since, after a certain period of time, Fikret Abdic appeared on the scene and proclaimed the autonomy of western Bosnia -- the area of Cazin, Kladusa and Bihac. Therefore, on the one hand, we had a public expression of determination to support a unified Bosnia on the part of Croatia, whereas, in fact, we were following in Milosevic's footsteps, because of what Milosevic had done, and this was fatal precisely for the Croats, because, due to it, 850,000 Croats -- the majority of 850,000 Croats have moved from Bosnia-Herzegovina so that there are only about 350,000 left in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So, after President Tudjman returned from the meeting at Karadordevo with President Milosevic, he informed you that Bosnia would be partitioned -- partitioned between Croatia and partitioned between Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly, from what he said, one could deduce that Bosnia could not survive, that we would be given the borders of the former Banovina plus Kladusa and Bihac -- Cazin and Bihac. That was the conclusion that could be drawn from what he said. Of course, nothing was said to the effect that there was a written document about it, or a written contract. That was not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr Mesic, could you tell the judges about any mapping commissions that were then set up between the Serbs and the Croats to agree on the boundary lines of a divided Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that, at the time, there was no debate about the Croat and Serb territories in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but there is no doubt that something started to happen which was not revealed to the public, namely, we were at war with Serbia, and, to me, it seemed abnormal for Serb and Croatian delegations to visit one another and especially during those visits a debate to be conducted on the territory of a third State, i.e., of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Reports reached me that there were people assigned to dealing with this problem of maps, geographical maps, to delineate the areas of Croats, Serbs and Bosniaks. On the Croatian side, several people participated, but, after a couple of months, they would give up the job, dissatisfied. Among them were Professor Lerotic, Dusan Bilandzic and others, who would abandon these talks, because they said, "This simply cannot be done," because Bosnia-Herzegovina is like a leopard skin -- the people are scattered throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that there is not a single locality that is ethnically pure, except for parts of Herzegovina, which could be said as being more or less purely Croatian -- even compared with areas in Croatia, there are few that are so ethnically pure as western Herzegovina is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr Mesic, could you describe a meeting that took place in Graz between Mate Boban and Radovan Karadzic, that meeting that took place on 6 May 1992 -- can you tell the judges about that meeting, and what Mr Boban told you following that particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time I was president of the executive board of the HDZ, and I was not informed about that meeting -- at least, I was not informed about it beforehand, and I learned about it having taken place quite by chance. For me, it was an absolute surprise, because there was a conflict between the Croats in Bosnia, and Karadzic -- because he was an exponent of Milosevic, we were at conflict with Serb policy and then suddenly such a meeting was held in Graz. Therefore, some time later I learned about that meeting and I asked Mate Boban what he could tell me about that meeting. He said, "Not much -- not much was signed at the meeting, but at least we now know that the Croats and Serbs have cleared up all dilemmas and no disputed issues remain. There is absolutely no further reason for conflict between the Serbs and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina." After some time -- again I happened to be at President Tudjman's -- he asked me to stay for lunch. At that luncheon, in addition to representatives of Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina, Nikola Koljevic appeared, too, who was at the time Vice-President of the Serb Republic, and it so happened that he sat next to me. We did not talk about Bosnia. He is a scholar of Shakespeare, so we talked about Shakespeare; people were shedding their blood in Bosnia-Herzegovina and he spoke to me about Shakespeare.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr Mesic, did you become aware after the Karadordevo meeting and after the meeting in Graz that cooperation between the Serbs and Croats in Bosnia was in fact occurring? For example, did you learn about the blockage of weapon supply to the siege of Sarajevo by Bosnian Croats and did you learn about events relating to Fikret Abdic's obtaining gasoline supplies and supplying that to the Serbs and any other events that would illustrate the increased cooperation between the Serbs and the Croats in Bosnia? Could you describe to those to the court, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As soon as the conflicts started between the Muslims or the Bosniaks on the one side and the Croats on the other, the assistance to the Bosnian army was intercepted, because all that aid could only come from Croatia. I must say that, at first, this cooperation was good, but it worsened with time. I know a concrete case, when -- he was not the imam of Zagreb, but I do not exactly know his title -- anyway, Sefko Omerbasic came to see me with a group of Muslims and said they had collected weapons and sent it, escorted by the Croatian army to Sarajevo, but that those weapons did not reach Sarajevo but were detained in Busovaca and that it was still in Busovaca, even the soldiers were still there, and this had been done by Dario Kordic. I called up Mate Boban and asked him to intervene, to let this shipment pass, because I realised that if Sarajevo is not defended, Bosnia would fall, and then the survival of Croatia would be in jeopardy. Mate Boban told me that he could not exert any influence over Dario Kordic, if he refused to do that, and then I joked and said, "What should be done?" He said, "Kill him". Following this joke, Tudjman called me after a short time and asked me, "Did you give instructions for Kordic to be killed?" I said, "no, I was joking, but some pressure had to be brought to bear on them. Both of them are in the HDZ. This one is his superior so the problem has to be resolved". How it was eventually resolved in concrete terms, I do not know. As for the gas or the petrol, I think that Fikret Abdic had a double-track policy. One was his communication with Croatia through which he could only receive the goods that he purchased abroad, including oil. What he did after that with the oil -- surely he could not have consumed all that he purchased himself, but at the same time he was cooperating with Belgrade and he appeared at the same time in both Zagreb and in Belgrade, and, finally, he established cooperation with Karadzic and, together with his forces, he attacked Bihac, when the very survival of Bihac was at risk, which meant the survival of parts of Bosnia. And I think that Croatia played a positive role in that particular instance, and this part of Bosnia was saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr Mesic, can you inform the judges what President Tudjman's view and what Slobodan Milosevic's view was in respect of shifting populations and what impact that would have on the division of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since I was Belgrade and had occasion to meet with Slobodan Milosevic quite a number of times, I think I can say, with objectivity, that I comprehended his policy. I realised what it was he wanted. Actually, when he was withholding the autonomy of Kosovo and Vojvodina, he proceeded from the position that Serbia must be unified, that it must not consist of three parts, and, in doing so, he was also undermining Yugoslavia, because, as I said yesterday, he was not interested in any kind of Yugoslavia, federal or confederal. This can be corroborated by the fact that we, in Croatia and Slovenia, had proposed a confederal model for a limited time of 3 to 5 years to see how it would work and if it worked, we could go on together. If not, we would part ways, but things would be decided similarly to the Czechs and the Slovaks. Milosevic obviously wanted something else. We see now the results of his policy. He wanted a greater Serbia, he wanted to extend the borders, and to take advantage of the collapse of Yugoslavia, to extend the borders of Serbia. However, his model included a policy of genocide, because he not only wanted a greater Serbia, but he wanted a purely Serb Serbia, and that is why his squadrons of death destroyed and killed everything they came across. They destroyed Catholic churches, Muslim mosques -- they simply wanted to erase all traces of other ethnic groups having lived in the areas through which his armies passed. The world was rather tolerant towards this policy of Milosevic's, and I assume that Tudjman drew the conclusion from this that the world wanted a division of Bosnia-Herzegovina and he obviously played the card of expanding his own borders, because he stated on a number of occasions that what we were holding by force of arms, when the war ended, sooner or later, it would belong to us. He was not very explicit. He did not say that this would be Croatia. He said it would be "ours". This could be interpreted as being Croatia, or Croatian territory over which the Croats would have certain privileges or priority. So, I think this is up to us to make our own conclusions, because he was not quite explicit. We can see what was really wanted from Hrvoje Sarinic, who was chief of cabinet of President Tudjman, who said in public that he went to meet with Milosevic 13 times, that he travelled to Belgrade while we were waging war -- a fierce war against the Serbs and he said that Serbia must emerge from the war as the small greater Serbia; in other words, the maximum ambitions of Serbia would not come true, but that what one could expect and what would be normal is for Serbia to make some territorial gains after this war. Therefore, if it was acceptable that, at the expense of a third party, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbia should emerge enlarged in terms of territory, how then could it be assumed that a little of that territory would not belong to Croatia as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did Franjo Tudjman also believe that, by shifting populations from the areas that had been allotted to it following the Karadordevo meeting, that that would benefit Croatia by dividing Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since, as I have said, Bosnia and Herzegovina is rather like a leopard skin in terms of population, with the exception of a few enclaves, it was difficult to establish ethnically pure territories and probably that was why Milosevic's genocidal policy was to cleanse areas, and people fled as soon as villages were torched and towns and people killed -- after all, hundreds of thousands of people were killed, so, clearly, this provoked fear, even among the people who had still not been swept up by the war. I remember an expression that was widely in use after the Vance-Owen Plan, which established the boundaries of the cantons in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and a term that became current was "humane resettlement". It is not a good idea for people to suffer and to tolerate this destruction -- it would be better for the people to be allowed to move towards their ethnic centres -- on the one hand there was Sarajevo, on the second Mostar, the third Banja Luka, but from today's optics, there is no such thing as humane resettlement. It is only a milder term for genocide, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you hear those discussions about the humanitarian resettlement of population personally and did you hear those -- that expression used by President Tudjman in discussions with Dario Kordic, in discussions with Mate Boban, Anto Valenta, Ignac Kostroman and others from Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because when talking to these gentlemen that you mentioned and when Tudjman used the term "humane resettlement", in explaining it, he said that this was to avoid suffering, to put an end to the killing, to put an end to the destruction, so that people should be given a chance to deal with the problem themselves, to swap houses among themselves and, actually, to end the war. But, ultimately, this led to division.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr Mesic, I would like to turn your attention now to the creation of Herceg-Bosna, which was proclaimed on 18 November 1991. Did you have occasion to see excerpts from the Narodni lists and other decisions from Herceg-Bosna, which vested the HVO with the executive power in the municipalities in which they were located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I somehow gained possession of these decisions that you are referring to. Those decisions were worded in such a way as to indicate the abolition of the legally elected authorities at the previous elections in the towns and municipalities and, instead, deputies were appointed by the HVO. I asked Mate Boban, who was the most senior among the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, I said that this was not legitimate, that it was not lawful, that the HVO could not abolish legally elected bodies, but the legally elected bodies could potentially set up some sort of institutions which might assist in the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Of course, those decisions never made any mention of Bosnia-Herzegovina but rather of Croatian lands, and I asked them what had prompted them to pass such decisions which are rather like a putsch, like a coup, they were not legal or legitimate. He said, "Look here, these were done by the most qualified lawyers, Vice Vukojevic from Zagreb, Smiljko Sokol, a university professor, and as regards the wording and the legal grounds, everything is absolutely above board, and do not worry, we will not make a mistake". As I was not satisfied with this answer, I asked President Tudjman whether he had seen these decisions that were being passed by these people in Herzegovina and he said that he had been informed about them. I repeated to him what the problem was. I was saying that, "Illegal organs were substituting for legal organs". He said that he agreed with me. After that, I tried to learn whether any changes took place, since he said he agreed with me, but no changes were made. True, due to certain operations taken by Vice Vukojevic, who was a member of Parliament, in my Parliament, I insisted several times with him that his status be cleared up, because he was one of the mediators in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then Tudjman said, "Leave it -- as far as Bosnia is concerned, all the civilian affairs are under the control of Vice Vukojevic and the military affairs by Gojko Susak the Defence Minister of the Republic of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: As a result of those decisions that you saw, Mr Mesic, what happened to the borders between Bosnia and Croatia -- did they exist or did they cease to exist, in your view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether even now that border is fully established. For a time, it did not exist at all -- it was an open border, and of course economically this was harmful for us, but the areas which were under the control of the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, our currency was in use, as an established currency, and the whole legal system was a replica of the Croatian legal system, so that one could not cross the border without any formalities at all. That border did not exist and, as far as I hear now, it is being established, but I am not familiar with the real state of affairs today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr Mesic, when you talked to Mr Boban about the putsch, as you described it, did Mr Tudjman agree with the decision to place HVO officials in authority over elected officials in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say that President Tudjman agreed with my opinion. He said that I was right, but he also said that I should not interfere with Bosnian affairs any longer, but that other people would be in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, in your opinion, Mr Mesic, that the leaders of Herceg-Bosna took their political direction from the leadership in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, and I can assert with certainty, that the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina was under the total leader of the HVO leadership in Zagreb, because any decision that needed to be made within the framework of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina had first to be established in Zagreb and any observer of the Croatian TV programme at the time could see that HDZ representatives would come to Zagreb every couple of days to talk with the President of the HDZ of Croatia. Afterwards, when the Republic of Herceg-Bosna was formed, representatives of the Croatian Republic would come, but they were the same people, and now, now that the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna no longer exists formally, representatives of the Croatian people come to Zagreb for instructions. I can concede that, during those discussions, it is possible to have a conflict of opinion, but since I do not participate in them, and I am familiar what the situation was before, it is my view that all they do is come to collect instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr Mesic, let me ask you to go back to the time when Herceg-Bosna existed initially in Bosnia. You have testified that you saw certain leaders from that entity, Mate Boban, Dario Kordic, Valenta, Kostroman and others come to Zagreb --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kostroman, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- come to Croatia and meet with President Tudjman. Where did they meet with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of those who came to see President Tudjman go to the presidential palace. It is always like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And would the meetings that occurred between President Tudjman and the people I have just mentioned, Boban, Kordic, Valenta, Kostroman and others be recorded in appointment books kept in the presidential palace?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can describe how these meetings are held. First of all, each meeting is recorded, every meeting is recorded -- is registered with the secretariat and then everything is recorded on the tape and President Tudjman also makes his own notes about the contents of some major meetings. We were always warned that other meetings were being taped and that everybody who was speaking should introduce themselves so that the person who is taking down minutes later would be able to identify each of the speakers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, is it during one or more meetings that you heard President Tudjman say, "What we hold with weapons will be ours"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I said this to several of those meetings. Of course, the discussion was also about where the Croatian forces were, what areas they were in. However, whether the President meant that this was going to be Croatia or this was going to be Croatian lands in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was no analysis of that. It was just said, "This was going to be ours", but what he actually meant by those words, I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you hear President Tudjman utter those words to the leaders of Herceg-Bosna in the context of discussions with the Vance-Owen peace plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was precisely around this time that these discussions took place, because the proposition of the Croatian side was to implement this agreement -- actually, this plan -- the Vance-Owen Plan -- as soon as possible, because it suited the Croats. However, it was still not signed by the Serbs, and later -- actually it was signed eventually, but it was never ratified by the Croatian assembly, so that the plan fell through. However, the Croatian side in Bosnia-Herzegovina enthusiastically supported the implementation of this plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you your opinion, Mr Mesic: In your opinion, would it be fair to say that the leaders from Herceg-Bosna, that is, Mate Boban, Dario Kordic, Valenta, Kostroman, and the military leaders of that entity Herceg-Bosna became instruments of implementing the policies of President Tudjman in Bosnia, particularly the policy to divide Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Compound, your Honour, and vague. If more clear, express terms could be used. We have been hearing about political leaders and now counsel wants to lump presumably every military leader in Herceg-Bosna into one group. I would ask that the question be clear and be broken down so we can have a fuller response by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, objection sustained. It was a very broad question. We see what you are trying to get, but try to do this in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question,

utterances.speaker: MR. MESIC
utterances.text: in your opinion, is it fair to say that the political leaders who I have identified, that is, Boban, Kordic, Valenta, Kostroman and others, became, in your opinion, instruments of implementing the policy of President Tudjman to divide Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact, in the final analysis, it was really on the Bosnia policy that I parted ways with President Tudjman. I had other objections, too. It was about centralisation of power at all levels, the centralisation of finances, the transformation of the so-called social property -- all these were issues which I parted ways with Tudjman's policies, but I think that Bosnia was really the dot over the "i", if you will, because I believe that Bosnia could not be divided, and it was this insistence on the division on the ethnic purity of Bosnia, the insistence on resettlement of the Muslim population from all towns -- from many towns in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- I thought that was a mistaken policy and I believe that those who implemented such a policy were really the instruments of a misguided Croatian policy in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did you believe that Kordic and Boban and Valenta and Kostroman were the instruments by which that policy of dividing Bosnia was implemented?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is this a different question? It is a different question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in a certain way, I had good relations with Mate Boban -- not with the others. I only met them during the official meetings, and he told me -- every time I met him I gave him my objections about this policy towards the Muslims, because I believed that we had a single aggressor in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that we will receive international support if the international community understands that there is a single aggressor, that that is Serbia, that this was not a civil war, and later the growing tensions and later the conflict with the Muslims really played into the hands of the Serb politics, or the Milosevic politics. I then asked him what was his politics. Then he said he had none himself, that he was really implementing the policies of Zagreb and that he only trusted Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mate Boban was the Commander-in-Chief of the military forces in Herceg-Bosna; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct -- this was so in legal terms -- this was the case in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the policies of Mate Boban were implemented in Herceg-Bosna by military force; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could we have a foundation -- a foundation for the answer? How does he know? Was he there, was he briefed? Could we just have a foundation for this, and some specificivity as to Central Bosnia as opposed to just referring to Bosnia-Herzegovina -- where?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are not going to ask questions about every question asked, but I would like Mr Harmon to be specific in this question. Ask your question differently, Mr Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were the policies of Mate Boban implemented through the use of military force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since Mate Boban was the President of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, he had the supreme political authority. He represented Bosnia-Herzegovina and obviously he was responsible for all the bodies of authority that were established in Herceg-Bosna, including the military ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of a single military leader in the HVO disagreeing with the principles and the policies of Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not meet these people, or, if I did, this would be in some joint meetings and I never talked to them, except with those who were in the Croatian army and who were going to Herceg-Bosna, that is to Bosnia-Herzegovina. I talked quite a bit with Slobodan Praljak and we could not come to agreement over this major issue, because he believed that no communal life could be preserved with the Muslims and that these two ethnic groups should go each their own ways and I talked to some others, who went to Bosnia -- to Herceg-Bosna, but these were just casual meetings, sort of in passing. I had no official contacts with these persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention, Mr Mesic, to the situation of dual citizenship and the situation of people who were citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina being able to be members of the Croatian Parliament, or the SABOR. Could you explain to the judges the laws I referred to, when they were promulgated and what their effect was on the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At any rate, I was part of the opposition politicians in Croatia who were against the election rule where citizens of other States could also participate, because I thought that only those Croats from Diaspora could take part in elections who happened to find themselves abroad at the time. As far as the citizen law, the electoral system allows all Croatian citizens to vote for the Croatian Parliament, and then the law provides that all Croats of -- all persons of Croatian origins could become citizens, with some provisions which were -- conditions that were easy to fulfil. There were 12 representatives in the Parliament, so about 10 per cent of the representatives in the Parliament came from Diaspora and it was clear that these Croats were Diaspora who have nothing to do with the Croatian State -- they did not pay any taxes -- it was clear that these were dominated for the most part by the HDZ, and so it was clear to me that this was sort of an abuse of the elections, because the Party that controls those 10 per cent of the vote clearly has a 10 per cent advantage coming into an election, and obviously it was something that the Opposition fought against. However, it is clear that the HDZ has an advantage here -- they have a monopoly -- they had a monopoly, so they passed this law. But in terms of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it had a devastating influence there, because what it did there, it oriented the Croats in Bosnia towards Croatia, rather than directed them to look for their happiness and future in the State where they were born, and where they lived with other people with whom they should look for co-existence. I also spoke to the representatives of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo, because I went there as well several times. They said that they did not want to exacerbate that problem, because they were getting all their assistance through Croatia, and so they did not want to undermine this kind of situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: As a result of that law that permitted people from abroad to be elected to the Croatian Parliament, were there members of the SABOR who were also involved in the fighting in Bosnia-Herzegovina, who were officers in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that several of these prominent members of the HDZ who took part in the Government of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina are legally members of the Croatian Parliament, so at the same time they are members of the Croatian Parliament and the one in Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, it is not easy for me to sort of estimate what the level of their involvement over there was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Harmon, we might now take a 20-minute break and then resume at 10 after. (3.50pm) (A short break) (4.17pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Harmon, until 5.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr President. Mr Mesic, you were President of the SABOR, which was the Croatian Parliament, from the end of 1992 until through 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While you were President of the SABOR, during that time, were members of the SABOR, who were from Bosnia-Herzegovina, also members of the HVO and of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never officially received any information from any representative that they were members of the HVO. However, I saw some people on television, including Vice Vukojevic and Ivan Tolj, wearing the HVO uniforms. I think there was a physician involved as well, but I think he was only involved in medical affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe a conversation that you had with Vice Vukojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since I was interested in the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the final analysis the defence of Croatia depended on what was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so, in that light, I called Vice Vukojevic. He was born in Herzegovina. I asked him what was actually going on there, expecting to hear a common defence was being established there. However, to my surprise, he said that it was impossible to work with Muslims, that there were conflicts in Prozor -- so much so, that they loaded them up on a truck. I said, "How many Croats were killed?" "None." "How many were wounded?" "None." I said, "What did you do? You just shot summarily people who were tied up?" I threw him out of the office and we never met after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Vice Vukojevic, did he representative himself to you as being a member of the HVO, or did you ever see him in a uniform belonging to the HVO while he was a member of the SABOR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only on television. I saw him only on television in uniform and he publicly said that he was a brigadier of the HVO. I do not know who appointed him to that position, but throughout this time he was also in the Croatian Parliament -- he never said that he was going to resign from that post in order to assume another one elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr Mesic, who was Ivan Tolj and what rank did he tell you he had in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what rank he held in the HVO. He was a general in the Croatian army. He was in charge of political affairs -- he ran the political affairs in the Croatian army and he said he had the same job in the HVO, but he was also a member of the Lower House of the Croatian Parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr Mesic, what is your conclusion as to the effect that this kind of representation in the SABOR had, that is, allowing people who were from Bosnia and Herzegovina to be members of the SABOR -- what effect did that have on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am convinced that this led to destruction -- if Croats were looking for their place in Croatia, they were not going to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina, they were not going to advocate the unity of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I thought that it was a policy that was detrimental to Bosnia-Herzegovina and I thought that it hurt Croatia as well. I have always believed, and I do so now, that, had it not been for the Washington and Dayton Accords, that it is questionable whether, with the fall of Bosnia, Croatia itself could have survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, while you were in the SABOR, did you send a commission down to Mostar to investigate into tensions -- I am sorry, into the events and the tensions that were rising between the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Different information, different news was reaching me as to what was going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina. For instance, in Mostar, and in order to get to the real information, I sent a delegation of our Parliament to Bosnia-Herzegovina, with a special visit to Mostar in order to find out what was really going on there, and it was led by Drago Krpina. Upon their return, they were very disappointed, they were very depressed -- they said the place was going to blow up, that a large number of Muslims of the villages surrounding Mostar left those villages, and those were mostly the Muslims who had fled the Serb terror, and they came to this area and that changed the complexion, the demographic complexion of Mostar, that this was upsetting the balance there, and that the leadership of the HVO was very concerned, because if such a large number of Muslims stayed in the area, they had feared that the conflict may arise from it and then later on television I saw that some people were leaving Mostar, moving out. The television showed columns of people leaving Mostar. I do not know where they were headed. Some were transported in trucks. I also do not know where. I asked Drago Krpina to inform President Tudjman about what was actually going on there, but I do not know what he actually did about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did in fact conflict break out between the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. A fierce conflict broke out, of terrible proportions, so that a part of Mostar now looks like Hiroshima. After the fighting, the city was divided. In principle the city was divided in an artificial way, and great efforts are being invested in order to establish an homogenous community, that the people there are Mostar citizens regardless of which ethnic origins they are of. There was even an old bridge there, which was a symbol of the city, which was destroyed. This bridge was built during the Turkish rule, but it was a symbol of binding of people, because it was a symbol of tolerance; the Turkish engineers designed this bridge, but it was built by the Croat workers with stone which was brought from Croatia. So, it was symbolic, the destruction of this bridge, which strategically meant nothing, and this was the justification for its destruction. I think that the policy was such that it wanted to destroy all bridges between the ethnic groups in Bosnia, to divide them as soon as possible, and to keep them as separate as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Which side of the conflict destroyed the Mostar bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to say who destroyed it, because I do not have personal knowledge of who did it, but I have information that this bridge -- that the destruction of the bridge was planned from the Croatian side. However, who issued the order, I do not know. There were different accounts in the public, but I do not think that the investigation of that was ever completed. However, objectively speaking, the Bosniak side had the least interest in destroying it. There are acts of provocation -- there are all kinds of thing in the war. An objective investigation would probably yield results.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In your opinion, Mr Mesic, was it logical for the Muslims to have started the Bosnian/Croat conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since I, too, am some kind of a general of the Croatian army, true, I attended military school for officers in reserve a long time ago, but I see no logic there, regardless of what the various sides allege. The Bosniaks were absolutely inferior in relation to our common aggressor and that is Serbia and its army. By the time when the Muslims had vast casualties, when more than 100,000 people were killed, and then for them to open up a new front and to narrow down the manoeuvring space that they had seems strange. First of all, they could get logistics from Croatia and, if they open up a front against the Croats, there is no assistance for them -- nor is there any chance for Bosnia to be saved. That is why it is unconvincing for me to claim -- it has no ground to claim that the Muslims started that war. However, it was harmful equally to the Croats and Muslims, and fortunately the Washington agreement came, and the Dayton Accords were signed which halted that war; but, to heal the effects of that war will take a long time yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr Mesic, during that war, did Croatia provide material assistance to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since the policy was that the HVO was defending Croatian interests and Croatian areas in Bosnia and Herzegovina -- because you must listen to the statements made by the leaders of Herceg-Bosna, they always spoke about Croatian lands, they never spoke about Bosnia-Herzegovina and this is something that bothered me in particular, so, clearly, Croatia did assist them and this was no secret. The only secret is how that assistance was organised. I was the President of the Parliament and I am familiar with the Croatian budget and there never was an item referring to assistance to Herceg-Bosna, nor was mention of Herceg-Bosna ever made in any way, but Josip Manolic, who abandoned the HDZ together with me, and he was in charge of all the intelligence services in Croatia, he stated in public, addressing the international and domestic public opinion, and he told me in person, that Croatia had spent 1 million German marks per day on assisting all the structures in Herceg-Bosna and that certainly means the HVO included, because, from where else would the HVO receive logistic support if not from Croatia. I think there is no secret there. I assume that the assistance came from the Defence Ministry to the Defence Ministry of Herceg-Bosna, the Ministry of the Interior to the Ministry of Interior of Herceg-Bosna. That is probably how that assistance was run, but I cannot explicitly allege how much was spent on this assistance, nor how it was actually channelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In your opinion, Mr Mesic, would the ministries that you have just described have kept records and maintained records of the assistance that it provided to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have never seen any such document, but anyone who has control of any funds must have some kind of control mechanism over the spending of those funds. Therefore, this must exist somewhere in the documentation of any ministry, including the Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Defence. All I know is that an audit was carried out in most ministries, except in the most sensitive segment, where it has not been completed, so that neither the public nor the Parliament have been fully familiarised with the audit carried out of the operations of the Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr Mesic, between 1992 and 1994, for purposes of this question, were Croatian troops and Croatian police in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, I can claim, with certainty, that the Croatian army could not legally go to Bosnia-Herzegovina for the very reason that, for the use of the Croatian army outside the borders of Croatia, a decision of the Croatian SABOR was required. No such decision existed. If it did, I would have known about it, but whether any units were there, whether they were used in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is a different matter. There was an agreement between President Tudjman and Alija Izetbegovic during the Serb attack on parts of Dubrovnik and surrounding area. An agreement was reached where a part of the Croatian army defended the hinterland of Dubrovnik and entered the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but that was in agreement with the Bosnian President. However, due to the post I held, I was often exposed in the media, I often appeared on radio and television. People asked me questions to the effect whether our troops were in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I said that I had requested a report from the Defence Ministry about it and that the answer I received -- an explicit answer was that there was no Croatian troops on the territory of any other country, including the country of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But soldiers did come to me who were discharged because they refused to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Their parents would come to see me, too, for the same reasons, but officially, I was always told that if any Croatian soldier did go there, he went there as a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So, Mr Mesic, is your answer that there were or there were not Croatian troops in Bosnia between 1992 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe there were, but if they were, they were not there legally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were those troops involved in the conflict between the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since after the outbreak of the conflict between the Croats on the one side and the Muslims on the other, a certain shift was made to the detriment of the Croats, I received information that some aid was given in the form of volunteers to halt the Bosnian offensive. Whether these were real volunteers, what kind of units were used -- that is something that I never investigated myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge, Mr Mesic, did the Croatian army personnel, who were in Bosnia, suffer casualties, and would there be records of those casualties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As in any normal administration, there should be some kind of a record, especially about human casualties, so if Croatian soldiers died there, then there must be a document to that effect, because the families need to regulate their benefits. If soldiers were wounded, again, their disability benefits needed to be regulated. But it is a fact that in our press there was a lot of vagueness and, whenever somebody was killed, the report said where he was killed and where he fought for Croatia, but, for a certain number of casualties, the term used for some in the papers was "fell for their homeland" and I was told that this phrase was used for those who fell in Bosnia. But I must admit that I did not investigate this in any detail, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr Mesic, did any of the soldiers who came to you directly inform you that, while serving in Bosnia, they wore patches that said "HV" but they had been instructed to remove those patches and replace them with patches identifying them as members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was told to me by several people, that the task of all those going to Bosnia was to remove the insignia of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the judges what you know about the issue of joint commands, that is, commands between the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats, and what the view of Zagreb was in respect of that issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning of the aggression, clearly, the whole Yugoslavia army sided with the Serbs, together with all its logistic equipment and this part was under the control of Karadzic, or, rather, Karadzic was just the instrument -- the main planner and operator was Slobodan Milosevic. As regards the Bosnian army, it was partly all Bosnian, because 13 per cent of the members were Serbs and, also, there were Croats from other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially from Sarajevo in that army. It is also well known that, in the HVO itself, there were quite a number of Muslims, so that some units in the Sava River valley were predominantly Muslim even though they belonged to the HVO. One must ask whether it is possible to wage a war against an aggressor if there is no unified command and the Bosnians insisted that there should be a joint command, because that was the only way to decide tactically and operationally about certain military operations. The Croatian side agreed with this joint command, which would mean that both the HVO and the Bosnian army would be represented according to the share of the population, so that the term "united command" was never used, and without that, it is difficult to score any military victories.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr Mesic, what was the relationship between the Croatian army and the officers in command positions in the HVO? Can you tell the court whether members of the Croatian army went to the HVO, served in command positions and then returned back to the Croatian army and can you identify, by name, those individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Professionally, that was not part of my competencies. I was primus interpares -- I was the speaker of Parliament, but certainly, I had more information than many other people. Obviously, it was possible for me to obtain some more detailed information, but this information was also available to the public, so that there was this fluctuation -- Milivoj Petkovic, Ante Roso, Slobodan Praljak, General Tolj -- they were for a time in the HVO, then again in the Croatian army. Whether each time they regulated their relationship every time they went and came back, I did not try to establish. But one could see that, within a short period of time, they changed their positions. They were for some time in the HVO, then again in the Croatian army, but how this was regulated, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me return to the issue of joint commands. I have been asked by one of my colleagues to clarify one point, Mr Mesic. Did Zagreb reject joint commands, or did they accept the principle of joint commands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zagreb was in favour of a joint command, but not in favour of a unified command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn next to the issue of Ahmici and ask you, Mr Mesic, first of all, had you heard of the events that occurred in Ahmici in April of 1993 and, if you had heard of those events, did you make an enquiry as to whether or not any investigation had been conducted into the massacre at Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, the time you mention, I was on an official trip with the Croatian parliamentary delegation, and, while on that trip, I learned of the events in Ahmici. When I came back, I learned about the various brutalities that occurred -- the atrocities, that great crimes were committed, of which even children were victims, and certainly, as a Croat, I was not glad to see Croats committing crimes, and, deep down, I had hoped that the Croats had not done it. I asked Mate Boban who I met shortly after that whether he knew anything about it. He said that all those events had been provoked by a British officer, and that they had established something, but not sufficient information about it. Then I asked, what had they ascertained and who had committed the crime? He said they had firm evidence that this was committed by people wearing black uniforms. Then I asked him, "But then you did not understand me, Mate, I did not ask what colour uniforms they wore, but who was wearing those uniforms". His reply was, "That, we have not established and they could have been Serbs". Knowing this part of the country, I knew that Serbs could not appear there, and that it was obvious either that he himself did not know, or that he was not telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Since then, Mr Mesic, have you heard whether anybody has been prosecuted by the Bosnian Croat officials for the massacres at Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have not heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Have you heard whether anybody has been disciplined, or was disciplined in the HVO for the war crimes that were committed in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My work was such that such a report would not reach me through official channels, but I never learned anything to that effect privately, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr Mesic, thank you very much for your testimony. I have no additional questions. Mr President, I have concluded my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr Harmon. I turn now to the Defence. I do not know who is going to be the cross-examiner -- it is Mr Nobilo -- yes, we spoke about it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well, thank you, Mr President. Good afternoon, Mr Mesic. During the examination-in-chief, we heard the positions you held. Among others, the most important, if I am not mistaken, was that you were President of SFRY, or member of the Presidency of SFRY, Prime Minister of Croatia, Speaker of Parliament, and Secretary-General of the Party. Will you tell me, after leaving the HDZ, did you participate in the elections within another Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After leaving the HDZ, I participated in the formation of the Independents Democrats of Croatia, which was joined by 11 former members of the HDZ. After some time, as members of this Party, we joined the HNS, and I am now Vice-President of the HNS, but, due to circumstances, HND continues to exist headed by Josip Manolic, but I do not know what their membership is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But while you were President of the HND, did you participate in any elections as an individual or as a member of a Party on a list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was elected to the municipal assembly of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you compete for Parliament, for President of State, or something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did your Party compete to join the Parliament, HND?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and we won one seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What share of the votes did you win?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that the HDZ is an obstacle to democracy, that there is no democratic decision-making, there is a single Party attitude, that they have plundered property through transformation, that they are nationalists, et cetera. Could you tell me, when did HDZ develop these characteristics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think after the agreement in Karadordevo -- this destructive policy began.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And when did that take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 30 March 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So that Party has all these negative characteristics as of 1991; and when did you leave it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left it in 1993. Franjo Tudjman asked me to withdraw from the Parliament, because he could not reach any agreement with Slobodan Milosevic, because I had said somewhere that the Serbs themselves would hang him on Terazije Square in Belgrade. By then, I was already in deep conflict with official policy, together with my friends, who abandoned the Party with me. As you know, a step in politics is not taken just like that, but when conditions mature, so that my departure from the HDZ did not take place suddenly, but when I felt that I had a chance of winning greater support from the public -- rather than just leaving the Party and ending my career without achieving anything, due to which I had left the Party anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So, when did you leave the Party and form the HND?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was somewhere in April 1994. But the talks regarding my departure from the HDZ lasted a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ever since the agreement in Karadordevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the meantime, you held the highest positions in the HDZ. Do you consider yourself to be partly responsible for the way the Party developed and what it did in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do shoulder part of the blame and I must admit, as the public knows, that throughout that period I advocated a policy of a unified and integral Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I struggled for a maximum degree of democracy in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Apart from the replacement of Kljujic, did you ever participate in the work of any other body of the HDZ for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I attended another meeting in Sarajevo when the question of the election of Kljujic arose, after Mr Perinovic resigned, but I do not recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you remember when Kljujic was replaced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1992, because then I was President of the executive board of the HDZ, but I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was it in the first half of 1992, can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please correct me if I did not understand you well. After the second half of 1992 and the replacement of Kljujic, you did not take an active part in the work of the bodies of the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never participated in the work of those bodies. I could merely follow what was happening there, up to a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. In that case, I will correct myself. After Kljujic was replaced, you no longer followed directly the work of any body of the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did follow it, but I did not participate in the work of those bodies. I did follow, because I had a certain position in Zagreb. I was a member of the Presidency of the HDZ and the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina was not formally -- it was formally a separate Party but all decisions were taken by the HDZ leadership in Zagreb regarding what needed to be done in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But did you attend meetings of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina bodies after that, did you go to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They came to Zagreb. The whole HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina came to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: About the visits to Zagreb, at what sessions and talks between Tudjman and the key figures of the HDZ for Bosnia-Herzegovina did you attend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to say, because I do not know how many such meetings were held -- after I demonstrated my difference with the Croatian policy towards Bosnia-Herzegovina, I was not invited to those meetings. But, if I happened to be at President Tudjman's and people from Bosnia-Herzegovina came, or rather from Herceg-Bosna or from the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, then I would stay on and attend those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you give us an example -- what meeting, when it was held, who was present, what was discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, we would have to look at the TV and press reports. There was at least one meeting every month, so that they appeared on television more often than our own announcers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: My question is, regarding you, which meetings did you attend, when, who was present, and what was discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Representatives of Herceg-Bosna, or of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, would come frequently, in a group, whose members were announced -- Mate Boban, Lasic, Boras, Kostroman, Dario Kordic -- I do not know all their names -- they would all come for counsel from the presidential palace.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But you are not answering my question. I have understood that these people came to Zagreb, but my question is: were you in attendance at any of those meetings? If you were, could you describe it for us -- when the meeting was held, what you discussed? I am asking you about the meetings that you participated in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you had asked me that question earlier on, I would have looked through my notes to tell you which meetings I attended. Whenever I happened to be in the presidential palace, I would attend that meeting, regardless whether I was invited or not. Sometimes I was invited, sometimes I happened to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you describe any one of those meetings and place it in a time frame?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how many times I have to repeat it at least once a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And you attended each one of those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have answered that question, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Mesic, Mr Mesic, Mr Nobilo is very clear -- you can answer as you wish, but I think that the question was very clear. You said that you participated in those meetings. He asked you for a example of those meetings and what happened at those meetings. You can or cannot, you want to or you do not want to, but you cannot simply say, "I have already answered the question". I think you have not answered the question. Maybe you cannot answer that. That is not my problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I can answer that question. I think that I was quite explicit. The HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, their political leadership would come to meetings with the HDZ political leadership of Croatia. The meetings were attended by the people whose names I have listed, as well as by members of the Presidency of the HDZ of Croatia. I did not note down the dates of those meetings. As for what was discussed, first, when the referendum was discussed -- if you want an example, I will give you some examples. When the referendum was discussed, the referendum in Bosnia-Herzegovina, when a decision had to be taken whether the Croats should support an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina or whether they should not participate in the referendum, because the Serbs had already decided not to participate in the referendum, I must say that the representatives of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina were against the Croats participating in that referendum, and this decision of theirs was supported by President Tudjman and the majority of the HDZ in Zagreb, or, rather, the Croatian HDZ. I had quite a lot of trouble to persuade both Tudjman and HDZ members that, if the Croats did not participate in the referendum, and if the Serbs did not participate, the referendum would not succeed and Bosnia-Herzegovina would remain part of Yugoslavia and only after that was that decision changed. At what meeting this happened, I cannot tell you exactly, but, whenever any key decision was taken, there was always a previous meeting of the HDZ of Croatia, and of Bosnia-Herzegovina. When the Vance-Owen Plan was about to be implemented, even though it had not been signed by the Serbs or approved by their assembly, at one such meeting it was agreed that the Vance-Owen Plan should immediately begin to be implemented, because it was in the interests of Croatia, because it completed, it rounded off Croatian territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You cited an example of the referendum and when the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan was contemplated; were you present there as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Until when were you invited to these meetings, can you place it in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was invited less and less frequently and sometimes I would just simply see on television that a certain meeting was held. So, I would say, up until about the end of 1993 -- after that, not any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
